Solution 1 is the only one with a plausible answer, and I checked its key claim: n = 5 is impossible.

**Necessary condition.** Each operation turns exactly 3 white cells black, so the number of black cells is always 1 + 3k. Hence n² ≡ 1 (mod 3), which rules out every multiple of 3. This eliminates Solution 3's power-of-2 characterization (e.g. n = 6 is excluded, but n = 7 is not a power of 2 and should be checked separately).

**n = 5 is impossible.** Label cells (row, column) and track how the corner cell (1,5) can be covered. Its only 2×2 square is the one with top-left (1,4), containing cells 14, 15, 24, 25. Covering 15 requires that square to have exactly one black cell among 14, 24, 25.
- After the first operation on (1,1), the only legal move is on (2,2), which blackens 23 and 33 together.
- Blackening 14 always comes from squares (1,3) or (1,4), and (1,3) also blackens 24, so 14 and 24 end up black together. That makes the corner square unusable.
- Blackening 24 alone is impossible: square (1,3) also blackens 14, square (2,3) already has 23 and 33 black, and square (2,4) also blackens 25.
- Blackening 25 alone is impossible: square (2,4) also blackens 24.

So 15 can never be covered, and n = 5 fails. This removes 5 from the list that Solution 2 uses, so its sum of 300 is wrong.

**Checking Solution 1's set.** Its characterization is "n not divisible by 3, and n ≠ 5" (3 is already excluded by the mod-3 rule). The 20 smallest such n are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31. Their sum is 326. I verified n = 1, 2, 4 directly and n = 5 fails, but I did not verify that every other n in the list works. The characterization matches what I recall of this competition problem, though I'm relying on that recollection for the sufficiency part.

CHOICE: 1
